tracks.title: Describing data
tracks.summary: This path is for describing a batch of numbers before any test. You move from where the numbers sit, through spread and skew, to pictures of outliers and of how the shape compares with a reference distribution. The steps are one description built in layers: a center, averages for spread and shape, and then plots of that same shape.

steps.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
steps.note: Start here, because every later description depends on where the batch sits. The mean, the median, and the mode are three answers to that question, and they line up when the numbers are roughly balanced.

steps.title: Moments
steps.note: Once you have those three summaries, moments put them in one family. The mean is the first moment, an average of the values, and higher moments average powers of the deviations, so spread and shape get numbers too.

steps.title: Bessel's Correction
steps.note: Building on that second moment, the sample variance averages squared deviations from the sample mean. Using n in the denominator acts as if the mean were already known, and that makes the variance a little too small, so the usual correction divides by n − 1.

steps.title: Skewed Distribution
steps.note: That leads to a shape where those three summaries pull apart. A long tail drags the mean with it, so the mean, the median, and the mode sit in different places.

steps.title: Boxplot and Histogram
steps.note: Once you have that lopsided shape, two pictures show it. A histogram shows the pile of values, and a boxplot packs the same center and spread into a box and whiskers.

steps.title: Boxplot and Outliers
steps.note: Building on the boxplot, the whiskers mark how far a point can sit from the quartiles before it counts as an outlier. The fence is a multiple of the spread inside the box, so distance is judged against that spread.

steps.title: Q-Q Plot
steps.note: That leads from a few distant points to the shape of the whole sample. A Q-Q plot lines the sample's quantiles up against a reference distribution, often the normal, and a curve away from the straight line means the shapes differ.

tracks.title: Statistical reasoning
tracks.summary: This path is for the reasoning that turns a curve into a claim about a sample. You build the normal distribution, watch means settle into it, meet the chi-square distribution that comes from squared standard normals, and then read a confidence interval as a long-run coverage rate. One thread runs through the steps: a model for single observations, a sampling distribution for a summary, and the claim a sampling distribution can support.

steps.title: Building the Normal Distribution
steps.note: Start here so you see the normal curve put together before any sample is drawn. It is fixed by a center and a spread, and the next steps ask when a summary of data takes that shape.

steps.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
steps.note: Once you have that shape, the central limit theorem says why means so often have it. As each sample gets larger, the distribution of the sample mean settles toward the normal curve, whatever shape the raw observations had.

steps.title: Horowitz (1974) CLT Simulation
steps.note: Building on that theorem, Horowitz's 1974 simulation tells the same story as a repeated draw in class. The collection of sample means takes on the normal shape the theorem describes.

steps.title: Chi-Square Distribution
steps.note: That leads from means to squared values. Square standard normal draws and add them up, and the sum follows a chi-square distribution, the sampling model for a variance.

steps.title: Target Analogy of Confidence Intervals
steps.note: Once you have a sampling distribution, you can mark a range that covers the parameter in a stated share of samples. In the target analogy the parameter stays fixed and each interval is a shot, so the percentage describes the procedure over many samples.

tracks.title: t-test
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing two means when the population standard deviation has to be estimated from the data. You meet the heavier-tailed t curve that takes the place of z, then compare two separate groups, then two measures on the same people. The reference distribution stays the same; what changes is which scores are being compared.

steps.title: z-Distribution vs t-Distribution
steps.note: Start here, because both comparisons on this path use a t curve. When the standard deviation is estimated from the sample, the reference distribution has heavier tails than z, and those tails are heavier still in a small sample.

steps.title: Independent Samples t-Test
steps.note: Once you have that curve, the independent-samples t-test uses it for two groups that do not share people. Each person is in one group only, and the standard error combines the spread of the two samples.

steps.title: Paired Sample t-Test
steps.note: Building on the two-group test, pairing changes what is averaged. The two scores from each person become one difference, and that removes person-to-person variation before the mean difference is set against the t curve.

tracks.title: Statistical power
tracks.summary: This path is for the chance of detecting an effect that is really there. First you see power as the part of the alternative sampling distribution that falls past the cutoff set by the null, and then you watch that chance change with the effect and the sample. The two steps are one definition, and then the curve that shows how the definition moves.

steps.title: Statistical Power
steps.note: Start here, with the two sampling distributions the test is weighing. Power is the share of the alternative distribution that lands beyond the cutoff set by the null.

steps.title: Power Curve
steps.note: Once you have that share, the power curve follows it as the study changes. A larger effect or a larger sample moves the alternative farther past the cutoff, and more of it counts as a detection.

tracks.title: ANOVA
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing means across groups, with the two-group t-test as the starting case. You split total variation into a part between groups and a part inside groups, add a second factor and its interaction, and then look at the assumptions behind the F test. Each step uses that same split and asks it a wider question.

steps.title: From t-Test to ANOVA
steps.note: Start here, so ANOVA is the two-group t-test opened to more means. In the two-group case the t-test and ANOVA ask the same thing: whether the means differ by more than the scatter inside the groups.

steps.title: Partitioning Sum of Squares
steps.note: Once you have that question, partitioning the sum of squares is how ANOVA writes the answer. All of the variation equals the part between groups plus the part left inside groups, and F compares those two parts.

steps.title: Two-Way ANOVA
steps.note: Building on one factor, two-way ANOVA gives the variation two labels. Each factor has its own main effect, and the interaction is the pattern that appears in the combination of the two.

steps.title: ANOVA Assumptions
steps.note: That leads to the conditions for reading those F comparisons in the usual way. The standard account wants residuals that are roughly normal, groups with similar spread, and observations that are independent of each other.

tracks.title: Association
tracks.summary: This path is for how two variables move together, and for what that movement means in units of variance. You start with covariance, rescale it to a correlation, and square the correlation to get the share of variance one variable accounts for in the other. The last step stays with variance and takes the independent case, where separate sources add and the total is their sum.

steps.title: Covariance and Correlation
steps.note: Start here, because association begins as shared movement. Covariance records that movement in the units of both variables, and dividing by the two standard deviations turns it into a correlation on a scale from negative one to one.

steps.title: Variance Explained
steps.note: Once you have the correlation, squaring it turns the strength of the line into a share of variance. That square is the proportion of variance in one variable that the linear relationship accounts for.

steps.title: Additivity of Variance
steps.note: Building on shared variance, this step takes sources that are independent of each other. Nothing is shared between them, so each variance is kept whole, and the total variance is their sum.
